Hook: Walk down the cereal aisle of an American supermarket and you see dozens of brands, from flakes to puffs to clusters, in every colour. But look at who makes them. Around 1980, Kellogg sold about 42 percent of all the cereal Americans bought, General Mills about 20 percent, and General Foods, the maker of Post, about 16 percent. In 1972 the Federal Trade Commission charged the biggest makers with sharing a monopoly: no explicit agreement, but prices kept high and rivals kept out by a flood of new brands. After nearly a decade of hearings, a judge dismissed the case in 1981, finding collusion unproved.

The puzzle did not go away. Cereal makers earn large margins: on the Island's own cereal aisle, which this part builds, about 42 percent of each price is margin over the cost of making one more box. Is that collusion, firms agreeing, openly or tacitly, not to compete? Or is it differentiation: every brand a little monopoly, because no box is a perfect substitute for another, and each firm owning many brands that it prices together? The catch is that nobody outside the firms can see their costs. In 2001 Aviv Nevo answered the question without them. He estimated how shoppers substitute between brands, worked out what margins competition alone would produce, and found them close to the margins observed: no collusion was needed. His method came from a 1995 paper on cars, by Steven Berry, James Levinsohn and Ariel Pakes, famous for being hard to read. This part reads it.

So this part asks how you can tell whether a market is competitive when you cannot see anyone's costs. Does a concentrated industry mean market power, or just efficient firms that grew large? How do you estimate demand for hundreds of related products, with their prices tangled up in qualities you cannot measure? How do you go from demand to markups, to the effects of a merger, to the value of a new product? And what can production data, or a simple count of firms in towns of different sizes, reveal?
Economics, Built. Part forty-three: measuring market power.

This is the first part of Act Nine, the fields: each part takes one field of economics, its tools and its open questions, beginning with industrial organization. Here is the plan. The old way of reading market power from concentration, a game about two mergers, and how conduct can be identified. Demand for differentiated products, from the logit to random coefficients, derived. The estimator run on the Island's cars and on the real ones, then markups, Nevo's cereals, mergers and new goods. Production functions, markups from production data, and entry. Two dials, merger review in practice, and the frontier.
SCP: For thirty years after the Second World War, industrial organization had one organizing idea. Structure, conduct, performance: the structure of an industry, how many firms and how concentrated, shapes their conduct, how they price and compete, which shapes performance, the profits and margins they earn. In 1951 Joe Bain sorted forty-two American industries of the late 1930s by whether their eight largest firms made at least seventy percent of the output. In the concentrated half, profit rates averaged about 11.8 percent; in the rest, about 7.5 percent. Concentration, it seemed, let firms collude and raise prices, and the cure was to break them up or keep them from merging.

In 1973 Harold Demsetz pointed to another explanation. Suppose some firms are simply better: lower costs, better products. They grow large, so the industry becomes concentrated, and they earn high margins, because they are better, not because they collude. The Island can check the logic. Here are 300 industries with the same demand and 5 firms each, all competing in the same way, by choosing quantities as in Part twelve's Cournot game. They differ only in how unequal their firms' costs are. Plot each industry's concentration against its margin, and they rise together, with a correlation of 0.78. Yet conduct is identical everywhere: no industry colludes. Bain's correlation, on its own, cannot tell market power from efficiency.

Demsetz also suggested a test. Look inside industries. On the Island, a firm's margin rises with its share, because the large firms are the ones with low costs; the correlation is 0.93. If collusion raised prices, every firm in a concentrated industry, large or small, would earn more. If efficiency explains it, only the large ones do. Demsetz found the second pattern in American data, and the debate turned from correlations to conduct.

The Island's pattern is not an accident; it is algebra. In the Cournot game of Part twelve, each firm's margin equals its share of the market divided by the elasticity of market demand. Average over firms, weighting by their shares, and the industry's margin equals the sum of squared shares, the Herfindahl index, divided by the same elasticity. So concentration and margins move together whenever costs differ, with no change in conduct at all. Structure and performance are both outcomes; the causes are in costs and conduct. To measure market power, economists had to measure conduct directly.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: two mergers among five brands.

Your turn. The Island's cereal market has five brands, each made by a different firm. Two are sweet, Sun Flakes and Honey Puffs. One is nutty, Nut Clusters. And two are bran cereals, Bran Buds and Bran Twigs, which taste almost the same. Each box shows the brand's share of sales and its price. Two mergers are proposed. Merger X joins the two bran cereals. Together they have about a quarter of sales, and the usual measure of concentration, the Herfindahl index, rises by 344 points. Merger Y joins the two largest brands, Sun Flakes and Nut Clusters, with almost sixty percent of sales; the index rises by 1,736. Which merger would raise the merging brands' prices more? Pause, and choose.

The answer is X, and not by a little. After merger X the two bran cereals' prices rise by about 30 percent. After merger Y the two largest brands' prices rise by only 3 percent. Shoppers lose 8.3 percent of what they gain from the market under X, and 3.5 percent under Y. The merger that barely moves the concentration index does more than twice the harm.

Why? Think about what stops a firm from raising its price: shoppers leave. When Bran Buds raises its price, about 47 percent of the shoppers it loses buy Bran Twigs instead. Once the two are one firm, those shoppers are no longer lost, so the higher price pays. When Sun Flakes raises its price, only 8 percent of its lost shoppers buy Nut Clusters; most go elsewhere or stop buying cereal. The fraction of lost sales that goes to the merger partner is called the diversion ratio, and it, not the market share, decides how much a merger raises prices. But diversion ratios are facts about demand, and nobody publishes them. The next chapters are about estimating them.
Conduct: Chapter three. Conduct as a parameter.

If concentration does not reveal conduct, can prices and quantities? Suppose you watch an industry over many years. Demand shifts out, as incomes grow, and you record the price and quantity each year. Story A: the industry is competitive, and price equals marginal cost, which rises with output. Story B: it is a monopoly with flat marginal cost, which sets output where marginal revenue equals that cost. With the numbers chosen here, both stories give exactly the same price and quantity every year. A rising supply curve under competition and a markup under monopoly can look identical. The data cannot tell them apart.

In 1982 Timothy Bresnahan and Lawrence Lau showed what breaks the tie. Suppose something rotates demand, making buyers more sensitive to price, as a cheaper substitute appearing would. A competitive industry does not care about the slope of demand: it produces where demand meets its supply curve. A monopolist cares a great deal: more sensitive buyers mean a smaller markup. So the two stories now predict different prices and quantities: 6.00 against 5.33. Market power becomes a parameter that can be estimated, provided the data contain something that rotates demand and not just something that shifts it.

The idea became a method. Write the industry's pricing rule as price equals marginal cost plus a markup scaled by a conduct parameter, theta. Theta of zero is competition; theta of one is monopoly, or a cartel acting like one. Estimate theta like any other parameter. It needs a variable that rotates demand, and a model of marginal cost. Its trouble is that real industries sell many different products, and much rests on the shape assumed for demand. Measuring market power in the cereal aisle needed demand for many products at once.
Logit: Chapter five. The logit, the red bus and the nest.

The simplest version makes each buyer's idiosyncratic taste, epsilon, independent across products, with a particular distribution. Then Daniel McFadden's logit gives the shares in closed form: each product's share is e to its mean utility, delta, over one plus the sum over all products, the one standing for buying nothing. In 1994 Steven Berry noticed what this allows. Take logs, subtract the log of the outside share, and the mean utility appears alone: a linear equation in price and characteristics, with the unseen quality as its error. Price can then be instrumented, as in any linear regression. But look at the elasticities the logit implies. The cross-elasticity of product j's sales with respect to product k's price depends only on k's price and share. It does not depend on how similar j and k are.

The classic illustration involves buses. Commuters choose between a car and a blue bus, and split half and half. Now a red bus appears, identical to the blue one except for its colour. The logit treats it as a new product with its own independent appeal, and predicts that each option now gets a third: the car loses a third of its riders to a bus nobody needed. Common sense says the car keeps half, and the two buses split the other half. This is the independence of irrelevant alternatives: under the logit, the ratio of any two shares ignores every other option, so a new product draws from all others in proportion to their shares.

The same flaw matters for mergers. Take the game's market, and suppose Bran Buds raises its price. Under plain logit, its lost shoppers spread across everything in proportion to size: only 5 percent go to Bran Twigs, its near twin, and most stop buying cereal. Under the nested logit that generated the game, 47 percent go to Bran Twigs. A plain logit would have called merger X harmless. The assumption chosen for demand decides the answer.

The nested logit is the first repair. The economist groups products into nests that are likely substitutes, here sweet, nutty and bran, with not buying cereal as its own nest. Each buyer shares a taste for everything in a nest, so shoppers who leave one bran cereal tend to choose the other. One parameter, sigma, measures how strong that shared taste is: zero gives back the plain logit, and as it approaches one, products in a nest become perfect substitutes. The game used 0.6. The weakness is that the economist must draw the nests in advance, and every product sits in exactly one. A sweet bran cereal has to choose. The next chapter removes the need to choose.
BLP: In 1995 Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes let different buyers want different things. Add to each buyer's utility a term that varies across buyers: here, a buyer's own sensitivity to price, the average alpha less sigma times a random draw nu for that buyer. On the Island's car market, sensitivity averages 0.6 with a spread of 0.15. In their own study of cars, buyers also differ in how much they value size, power and air conditioning. The consequence is the point of the whole method. A buyer who chose an expensive car is, on average, a buyer who does not mind high prices, so when its price rises that buyer moves to another expensive car, not to the cheapest. Substitution follows similarity, without the economist drawing any nests.

What does this do to market shares? Each buyer still makes a logit choice, but with their own sensitivity, so each has their own probabilities of buying each car. Here are five buyers, from the least sensitive to price at the top to the most sensitive at the bottom: the first leans to the dear car, the last to the cheap one, or to buying nothing, the empty end of each bar. The market's share of each car is the average over all buyers: an integral over the distribution of tastes. It has no formula, so it is computed by simulation: draw a few hundred buyers, compute each one's logit probabilities, and average.

Now the hard part. The plain logit could be inverted by taking logs. With random coefficients, for any guess of sigma we need the mean utilities, delta, that make the predicted shares equal the observed ones, for every product at once. Berry proved that a simple rule finds them: add to each delta the log of its observed share minus the log of the share the current deltas predict, and repeat. The rule is a contraction, so it converges from any start. In one year of the Island's car market, starting from the plain logit's answer, each step shrinks the error by about the same factor. After thirty steps the deltas match the ones planted in the simulation to the last digit a computer keeps.

The whole estimator is a loop. Guess how much tastes differ, sigma. Invert the observed shares by the contraction, which gives the mean utilities for that sigma. Because the mean utilities are linear in price and characteristics, a linear instrumental-variables regression gives alpha and beta, and what is left over is the unseen quality, xi. Then check the moment conditions: the unseen quality should be uncorrelated with the instruments. If it is not, try another sigma. The estimate is the sigma that makes the moments closest to zero, the generalized method of moments. On a modern computer each pass through the loop takes a fraction of a second.

Which instruments? Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes used the characteristics of rival products. A car surrounded by close rivals must be priced lower, and its rivals' features were fixed years before, when the models were designed. They also used the characteristics of the firm's own other models, which it takes into account when pricing each one. Cost shifters, such as the price of inputs, move price without touching quality. And Amit Gandhi and Jean-François Houde later showed that measures of how crowded a product's neighbourhood is in characteristics space are stronger still. All of them rest on one assumption: that characteristics are chosen before the unseen quality shocks are known.
Cars: Chapter seven. BLP on the Island, then on real cars.

Does the estimator find the truth? On the Island we know it, because we planted it. Here are 40 simulated Islands, each with 40 years of 24 car models, priced by six firms competing in the way of Part twelve, with buyers whose price sensitivity averages 0.6. Plain logit by ordinary least squares finds a sensitivity of about 0.22 every time: far too low, because the expensive cars are also the good ones. Instrumenting price, with an input price and measures of how crowded each car's neighbourhood is, raises it to about 0.42: better, but plain logit is the wrong model, so even good instruments cannot rescue it. The full random-coefficient estimator is centred on the truth, at 0.60, with a wider spread: the price of a richer model estimated from forty years of data.

The difference shows in the elasticities. In green, each car's true own-price elasticity on one Island, against its price. Dearer cars face somewhat more elastic demand, but the buyers of dear cars are the less sensitive ones, so the rise is gentle. The plain logit, even with good instruments, makes the elasticity proportional to price: too low for cheap cars, too high for dear ones. Across the forty Islands the median elasticity is minus 3.87; ordinary least squares says minus 1.87, the IV logit minus 3.56, and the random-coefficient estimator minus 3.80.

Now the real thing: the data Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes used. 2,217 car models sold in the United States between 1971 and 1990, with prices, shares and characteristics. Plain logit by ordinary least squares says that 1,491 of them face inelastic demand, an elasticity below one. That cannot be right: a firm facing inelastic demand could raise its price, sell a little less, and earn more. Instrumenting price with the characteristics of each firm's other models and of its rivals' models, as they did, cuts the count to 726, with a strong first stage. Better, but still hundreds of impossible answers, which their paper also reports for simple specifications. Plain logit cannot describe this market.

There is a deeper problem, and it is the one that matters for market power. A single-product firm facing plain logit demand sets a markup, in dollars, of one over alpha times one minus its share, and with tiny shares that is just one over alpha. So the IV logit gives every car almost the same markup: about 7,300 dollars of 1983 money. The cheapest small car and the dearest luxury saloon, alike. With random coefficients the buyers of dear cars are the ones who care least about price, so dear cars carry larger markups, which is what Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes found. The flexibility is not a refinement. It is what lets the data, rather than the model's shape, decide where market power lies.
Markups: Chapter eight. From elasticities to markups: Nevo's cereals.

With demand in hand, markups follow. A firm selling one product sets its margin, as a share of price, at one over the elasticity of its demand: Lerner's rule from Part ten. A firm selling several products prices each one knowing that a higher price sends some shoppers to its other brands, which it does not mind. Its first-order conditions add those diverted profits. Stack the conditions for every product, with a matrix omega that records who owns what, and solve. The markups come out of demand and ownership alone. Costs are never observed; they are what is left: price minus markup.

Nevo's test turns this around. Take observed prices and estimated demand, and ask what margins each theory of conduct implies. Here is the Island's cereal aisle: twelve brands from four firms, with demand known. If every brand were priced by its own firm, the margins that would make today's prices optimal average 38 percent: that much comes from differentiation alone. With the real owners, each firm pricing its portfolio, they average 42 percent. And if all four firms acted as one, a cartel, today's prices would imply margins of 92 percent: a cartel would charge far more than this, so prices this low are hard to square with collusion.

Now compare with margins measured some other way. On the Island, split the margin into its sources: 38 points from differentiation, 4 from firms owning several brands, and another 50 that a cartel would add. The margin actually earned, which on the Island we know, is 42 percent: exactly what competition among multi-product firms predicts. Nevo did this for the leading American cereal brands, comparing with margins from accounting data. Differentiation and portfolios explained most of the margins. The industry's prices were consistent with firms competing, not colluding, despite the high margins that had made the Commission suspicious.

The method is powerful, and it rests on assumptions worth naming. Demand must be right: every error in the elasticities passes straight into the markups. Conduct is a hypothesis: competition among multi-product firms is tested against alternatives, not proved. The benchmark is rough: accounting margins mix the cost of one more box with average costs such as advertising. And economists also use other evidence, such as documents and sudden price jumps, as a story in chapter fourteen shows.
Merger: Chapter nine. Merger simulation and new goods.

Demand and conduct also predict what a merger would do, before it happens. The recipe has four steps. Estimate demand, which gives elasticities and the diversion ratios of chapter two. Recover each product's marginal cost as price minus the markup competition implies. Merge two firms: in the ownership matrix, their products now share an owner. Solve for the new equilibrium prices. Costs and demand are unchanged; only the incentives are new, because each merged brand now counts the sales it pushes to its new sister as kept, not lost.

Run it on the Island's aisle. The two smaller firms, with 43 percent of sales between them, propose to merge, and the simulation puts a number on the harm: the merging brands' prices rise by 5.8 percent on average. The Herfindahl index rises by 899 points, to 3,462: under the American guidelines, a merger presumed to harm competition. The rivals' prices rise too, by 0.4 percent, because with dearer competitors they can charge a little more. No collusion is involved; the merger simply changes what is privately optimal.

Mergers can also save costs, which pushes prices down. How large would the savings have to be? Gregory Werden's answer: find the marginal costs at which the merged firm would choose exactly today's prices. On the Island the merging brands' costs would have to fall by about 12 percent, brand by brand as shown. Savings that large in the cost of one more box are rare, and the agencies count only savings that are verifiable and specific to the merger, a standard that chapter fourteen's beer story puts to the test.

Demand also values new products, and here the logit's flaw becomes absurd. In the plain logit every product carries its own independent taste, so adding an exact copy of Nut Clusters, same box, same price, gives every shopper a gain worth 0.092 dollars, about 3 percent of its price, from the chance that they like the copy better. With the game's nests the gain is 0.035 dollars, and as products in a nest become perfect substitutes it vanishes, as it should. In 2002 Amil Petrin measured the value of the minivan, introduced in 1984. Adding information on who buys which car, families buying minivans, to the market data changed the estimated gains substantially; the plain logit overstated them. What a new product is worth depends on how it is different, and from whom it draws its buyers.
Production: Chapter ten. The supply side: production functions.

Markups can also be read from the supply side, but first we need production functions, which have their own famous problem. A plant's output depends on its labour and capital and on its productivity, omega, which the plant knows and the economist does not. Here are three hundred of the Island's 1,500 plants. Colour shows productivity. The productive plants, in gold, hire more workers, because each worker produces more there. So a regression of output on labour credits labour with productivity's work: ordinary least squares finds a slope of 1.00. The true elasticity, planted on the Island, is 0.6. This is the simultaneity problem, noticed by Marschak and Andrews in 1944: inputs are chosen with knowledge the economist lacks.

The modern fix uses the plant's own choices as a window on its productivity. Some input, such as materials, rises with productivity given the other inputs, so it can be inverted to recover productivity. Stage one regresses output on a flexible function of labour, capital and materials, stripping out pure noise. Stage two uses timing. Productivity is persistent, and its surprise this year cannot have been known when capital was installed last year, or when last year's labour was hired. Those zero correlations pin down both elasticities. Steven Olley and Ariel Pakes used investment as the proxy in 1996, studying telecommunications equipment after the break-up of AT and T; James Levinsohn and Amil Petrin used intermediate inputs; and Daniel Ackerberg, Kevin Caves and Garth Frazer showed in 2015 that labour's coefficient must come from the second stage.

On the Island's plants, the methods land in very different places. Ordinary least squares gives labour an elasticity of 1.00 and capital 0.14: labour takes productivity's credit, and capital, chosen a year earlier, gets too little. Comparing each plant with itself over time helps only partly, because productivity changes from year to year. Ackerberg, Caves and Frazer's estimator gives 0.60 and 0.30, against the truth of 0.6 and 0.3.

Estimating productivity this way revealed one of the series' facts. Within narrow American manufacturing industries, Chad Syverson found, the plant at the ninetieth percentile of productivity makes about 1.92 times as much output from the same inputs as the plant at the tenth. Why such gaps persist, from management to technology to which plants survive, is the subject of Part sixty-two. The Island's plants were planted with a ratio of 1.87, to match.
DLW: Chapter eleven. Markups from production data.

Demand systems need years of work for one industry. In 2012 Jan De Loecker and Frederic Warzynski proposed a way to measure markups for any firm from its accounts. A firm minimizing cost uses a flexible input, such as materials or labour, until its price equals its marginal product valued at marginal cost, lambda. Rearranged, the input's output elasticity equals its cost divided by marginal cost times output. Since the markup is price over marginal cost, it equals the output elasticity divided by the input's share of revenue. The elasticity comes from a production function, estimated as in the last chapter. The share comes from the accounts. No demand system and no assumption about how firms compete: any firm, in any industry.

The Island shows what the formula needs. Its plants were given markups around 1.3, and they spend on labour the share of revenue that cost minimization implies. With labour's elasticity from Ackerberg, Caves and Frazer, the formula recovers the markups almost exactly: median 1.30. With the elasticity from ordinary least squares, 1.00, every markup is inflated in the same proportion, to a median of 2.17. The ratio between firms survives a wrong elasticity; the level does not. And the level is what a debate about rising market power is about.

In 2020 De Loecker, Jan Eeckhout and Gabriel Unger applied the formula to every American public firm. The sales-weighted average markup was 1.21 in 1980, and 1.61 by 2016: from twenty-one percent above marginal cost to sixty-one. The median firm's markup barely moved. The rise came from the top: high-markup firms charged more, and sales shifted toward them. It fits the intermission's picture, profits after tax rising from about 6 percent of GDP between 1980 and 2000 to about 10 percent since 2010, though profits and markups are not the same thing.

The finding set off a debate that is still open. James Traina showed that counting selling, general and administrative costs as variable, as many modern firms' costs are, makes the rise much flatter. Stephen Bond and coauthors showed that with revenue rather than quantity data, the production-function elasticity is not the one the formula needs, as the Island just showed for a wrong elasticity. Public firms are not the whole economy. Susanto Basu's review found the broader evidence for a large rise in the typical firm's markup inconclusive. Whether the typical firm gained power, or sales shifted toward firms that always had it, is the open question, and the markups dial records where things stand.
Entry: Chapter twelve. How many dentists does a town need?

Sometimes market power can be read from the simplest data of all: how many firms there are. In 1991 Timothy Bresnahan and Peter Reiss studied about two hundred isolated towns in the western United States, far enough from cities that their residents bought locally, and counted the doctors, dentists, plumbers and other businesses in each. A town supports N firms while its population, times each firm's profit per resident, covers the fixed cost of opening. So the population needed for N firms is N times the fixed cost over the market's profit per resident. If each entrant makes competition fiercer, margins fall, and every additional firm needs more people per firm than the one before. If entry changes nothing, the population per firm stays the same. The ratio of successive thresholds measures how competition changes with each entrant.

The Island has 400 isolated towns of different sizes. Each dot is a town: its population across, the number of dentists up. Small towns have none or one; large ones have five or more. The pattern is noisy, because towns differ a little in what opening costs. Behind it are the thresholds planted on the Island. The market's profit per resident falls from one with a single firm to 0.6 with two and 0.48 with three, then hardly at all: competition arrives with the second and third firm.

Bresnahan and Reiss estimated the thresholds with an ordered probit: the chance that a town has at least N firms rises with its population relative to the N-th threshold. On the Island the truth says the second firm needs 1.67 times as many people per firm as the first, the third 1.25 times as many as the second, and after that about one. Estimated from nothing but populations and counts, the ratios are 1.77, 1.22, 0.99 and 1.02. For comparison, Cournot competition with straight-line demand would keep the ratio between 1.1 and 1.2, and a cartel would hold it at one. In America's towns Bresnahan and Reiss found the Island's pattern: competitive conduct changes quickly as the number of incumbents rises, most of the change comes with the second and third firms, and once a town has three to five, another entrant changes little.

Counting firms reveals another of the series' facts, at the scale of the whole economy. In 2001 Robert Axtell plotted the sizes of about five and a half million American firms and found Zipf's law: the number of firms larger than a given size falls in proportion to that size, with an exponent close to one, the same law that governed cities in Part thirty-seven. The usual theory is proportional random growth, with firms entering and exiting. Agora builds that economy of firms in Part fifty-two.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: merger review.

In America, mergers above a certain size must be notified to the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice, which can sue to stop them. Their guidelines begin with concentration. Since December 2023, a merger is presumed to lessen competition if it leaves a Herfindahl index above 1,800 and raises it by more than 100 points, or creates a firm with more than 30 percent of the market and raises the index by more than 100. Those are the thresholds of 1982, restored; from 2010 they were higher. Both of the game's mergers trip the screen, though one raised prices ten times as much as the other. The Island aisle's merger trips it too, with simulated prices 5.8 percent higher. The presumption can be rebutted, and the argument then turns to the tools of this part: diversion ratios, margins and simulation.

Between the index and a full simulation sits a test from Joseph Farrell and Carl Shapiro, upward pricing pressure. When product one's owner buys product two, raising one's price now keeps the profit on the sales diverted to two: the diversion ratio times two's margin. Against that, credit the merger with some saving in one's cost, say ten percent. For merger X: 0.47 times 0.59, less a tenth of 1.00, is positive, so prices are pushed up. For merger Y the pressure is gone: minus 0.060. The test needs no market definition and no full demand system, only diversion ratios and margins, which is why agencies use it as a screen.

Called it? In June 2008 the Department of Justice let SABMiller and Molson Coors combine their American brewing in a joint venture, MillerCoors. After an eight-month investigation it judged the venture not likely to lessen competition substantially, and its cost savings substantial and credible. The savings were real. Coors beer could now be brewed in Miller's plants, nearer its drinkers, cutting the average shipping distance by 364 miles, and Orley Ashenfelter, Daniel Hosken and Matthew Weinberg found that the savings offset, on average, the roughly 2 percent that higher concentration added to prices. But prices of MillerCoors and of Anheuser-Busch, its rival, jumped together soon after, and Nathan Miller and Weinberg estimate them 6 to 8 percent above what competition with those savings would give, consistent with the two leaders coordinating. The verdict: partly right. The review weighed the savings against each firm's own incentive to raise prices; the risk that fewer, larger rivals would follow one another's prices was harder to put a number on.

Who does this work? Economists at the agencies: the Federal Trade Commission's Bureau of Economics, the Justice Department's Economic Analysis Group, the European Commission's competition directorate, Britain's Competition and Markets Authority. Consultancies and expert witnesses on both sides of a case, who estimate diversion, simulate mergers and defend their numbers in court. In industry, pricing and strategy teams estimate the same demand systems to set prices and plan products, the subject of Part fifty-nine. And academics who study mergers after the fact, like the beer studies, which keep the simulations honest.
